requirement: The `habeas` skill MUST tell agents that a new project with little code starts with `habeas-requirements`, not `habeas-bootstrap-requirements`, even though most of its code has no references.
rationale:
The requirement has one obligation. The `habeas` skill MUST tell agents that a new project with little code starts with `habeas-requirements`, not `habeas-bootstrap-requirements`, even though most of its code has no references.

`tests/authoring_cli.rs#fn[the_habeas_skill_starts_a_new_project_with_the_requirements_skill]` is marked `{test}` for the requirement. It reads step 1 of the `habeas` skill's Workflow section through `step` and `workflow_steps`. These helpers parse the bundled skill's numbered workflow steps. The test then uses `assert_text` to require two phrases:

- The routing row "Adopting Habeas in an existing codebase, or most of the code has no references | habeas-bootstrap-requirements". This checks that the bootstrap skill is routed only for existing codebases or mostly unreferenced code.
- The sentence "A new project with little code starts with habeas-requirements, not habeas-bootstrap-requirements, even though most of its code has no references". This is the required statement: it names both skills and includes the "even though most of its code has no references" caveat.

`assert_text` uses `assert!(text.contains(phrase))` for each phrase, so the assertions enforce the content. The step lookup panics if the step or workflow is missing.

The requirement is a content statement in a bundled document. There are no input classes, boundaries, modes or failure cases to cover beyond the presence of this text. I found no gap.
